text:
This module has undefined behavior in three safe functions, debug panics and integer overflows on stock and price math, inventory updates that drop or double-allocate units, and a lock-order deadlock in `Service`.

### Memory safety

`SlotTable::lookup` (line 185) takes `slot` straight from a scanner message and calls `get_unchecked`. If `slot >= slots.len()`, including every lookup on an empty table, that is undefined behavior. The `unsafe` block sits inside a safe function, so callers can hit it with ordinary code. `assign` is bounds-checked; `lookup` is not.

`append_batch` (lines 194–196) saves `buf.as_ptr().wrapping_add(start)` and then calls `extend_from_slice(tail)`. `extend_from_slice` reallocates when the spare capacity is smaller than `tail`, which is what happens for any multi-SKU batch once `push` has filled the buffer. Reallocation frees the old allocation, and `*first` is a use-after-free. The first SKU is already in `head`; the pointer round-trip is what makes this undefined behavior.

`decode` (line 218) turns network bytes into a `String` with `str::from_utf8_unchecked`. Invalid UTF-8 is undefined behavior. The `Result` does not report it. Combined with the truncated length prefix below, a long name this crate encoded can split a multibyte character and trip the same unchecked conversion.

### Panics and overflow

`deltas` (lines 156–157) only works for an empty slice. The loop is `for i in 0..prices.len()` and the body reads `prices[i + 1]`. On a slice of length `n > 0` the last `i` is `n - 1`, so `prices[n]` panics. `deltas(&[10, 12, 15])` panics; the `Vec` capacity of `len - 1` is the count the loop should have produced. Earlier iterations also do a raw `i64` subtraction. `deltas(&[-1, i64::MAX])` overflows `i64::MAX - (-1)`, which panics in debug and wraps in release.

`Item::available` (line 47) is `on_hand - reserved`. When `reserved > on_hand` that panics in debug and wraps in release. `reserve` and `low_stock` both call it. In release the wrapped available count is huge, so `reserve` accepts the request and `reserved += qty` can overflow too. `on_hand` and `reserved` are public, so callers can break the invariant directly.

`record_loss` (line 120) does `on_hand -= lost` with no check against `on_hand` or against unreserved stock. `lost > on_hand` panics or wraps. A smaller loss still leaves `reserved > on_hand` (10 on hand, 8 reserved, lose 5 → 5 on hand and 8 reserved). `available`, `low_stock`, and `ship` then see a broken item. Those lost units are still reserved and can later be “shipped.”

`ship` (line 112) checks `qty > reserved` and then does `on_hand -= qty`. Once `on_hand < reserved`, shipping units that are still reserved underflows `on_hand`: panic in debug, wrap to a huge stock count in release.

`total_value` (line 127) computes `on_hand as u64 * price_cents` and sums the products in `u64`. The multiply or the sum panics in debug and wraps in release. One SKU with `on_hand = 3_000_000_000` and `price_cents = 10_000_000_000` overflows the product.

`place_hold` (line 253) evaluates `Instant::now() + ttl` after `reserve` has succeeded. A `ttl` that does not fit in `Instant` (for example `Duration::MAX`) panics. The `Hold` is never inserted, the units stay reserved, and unwinding poisons the `warehouse` and `holds` mutexes. Later `lock().unwrap()` calls panic as well.

`moving_average` asserts `window > 0`. That matches the stated precondition. The window sum is a `u64` and overflows only for a window of about 2^32 maximum-sized samples.

### Inventory logic

`receive` (lines 80–81) always `insert`s a new `Item` with `on_hand: qty` and `reserved: 0`. The comment says an existing SKU gains `qty` units. A second receipt replaces the previous balance and clears reservations. Those units become available again while any `Hold`s for that SKU are still live, so the same stock can be reserved twice. The next `confirm` then fails `ship` because `reserved` was zeroed.

`release` (line 101) uses `saturating_sub` and returns `Ok` when `qty` is above `reserved`. Reservations for one SKU share a single counter. Releasing more than one hold’s quantity clears the others too. Those units look available and can be reserved again while the old holds remain. `ship` reports this case as `Insufficient`; `release` does not.

`confirm` (line 260) `remove`s the hold before `release` or `ship`. Both return `Result`, and `?` returns immediately on error. The id is gone, so the caller cannot retry and `sweep_expired` will not see it. If `ship` returns `Insufficient`, the units stay in `reserved` with no hold left. `sweep_expired` (line 278) drops the hold even when the `release` result is discarded.

### Concurrency

`Service` uses three mutexes and two lock orders. `place_hold` (line 245) and `sweep_expired` (line 272) take `warehouse`, then `holds`. `confirm` (line 259) takes `holds`, then `warehouse`, and it keeps `holds` for the whole warehouse call. `std::sync::Mutex` does not recover from that cycle: one thread in `confirm` holding `holds` and waiting for `warehouse`, and another in `place_hold` or `sweep_expired` holding `warehouse` and waiting for `holds`, block forever. `place_hold` has already reserved the stock before it waits, so the deadlocked call also strands units with no map entry. `next_id` is only locked from `place_hold` and is not part of the cycle.

The existing tests cover one reserve/ship path, a short ASCII codec round trip, and a valid parse. They do not exercise these paths.

ISSUES:
L47: `available` computes `on_hand - reserved`, panicking in debug and wrapping in release when `reserved > on_hand`
L81: `receive` inserts a new item with `on_hand = qty` and `reserved = 0`, replacing an existing SKU instead of adding quantity
L101: `release` saturates `reserved` to zero and returns Ok when `qty` exceeds `reserved`, clearing every reservation on that SKU
L112: `ship` subtracts `qty` from `on_hand` after checking only `reserved`, so `on_hand` underflows when it is below `qty`
L120: `record_loss` does `on_hand -= lost` with no bounds check, panicking or wrapping and leaving `reserved` above `on_hand`
L127: `total_value` multiplies `on_hand` by `price_cents` and sums in `u64`, overflowing on large stock values
L156: `deltas` iterates `i` over `0..prices.len()` and reads `prices[i + 1]`, panicking out of bounds for every non-empty slice
L157: `deltas` subtracts `i64` prices directly, so large swings overflow (panic in debug, wrap in release)
L185: `lookup` uses `get_unchecked` on a scanner-supplied slot; an out-of-range index is undefined behavior
L196: `append_batch` dereferences a raw pointer into `buf` after `extend_from_slice`, which can reallocate and free that pointer (use-after-free, undefined behavior)
L204: `encode` stores `name.len() as u8`, truncating lengths above 255 and emitting a frame `decode` will misread
L218: `decode` builds the name with `from_utf8_unchecked`; invalid UTF-8 from the network is undefined behavior
L253: `place_hold` adds `ttl` to `Instant::now()` after `reserve`, and that addition panics when the deadline overflows
L259: `confirm` locks `holds` then `warehouse`, while `place_hold` and `sweep_expired` lock `warehouse` then `holds`, so concurrent calls deadlock
L260: `confirm` removes the hold before `release` or `ship` succeeds, so an error leaves reserved units with no hold id

I am reviewing the Rust inventory service module for real defects.

`Item::available` subtracts `reserved` from `on_hand` without checking bounds. If reserved exceeds on hand, this panics in debug or wraps in release.

`record_loss` can leave `on_hand` below `reserved`, which triggers the overflow in `available`. `receive` also replaces the entire item instead of adding to existing stock.

The doc comment for `receive` claims it adds units to existing stock, but the implementation replaces the entire item. This overwrites prior reservations and on-hand counts, so any existing stock or held units are lost.

`reserve` adds `qty` to `reserved` without checking bounds. The `qty > have` guard is ineffective because `have` is computed by `available()`, which already panics or wraps if `on_hand < reserved`. Thus `reserve` can overflow `u32` when the invariant is violated.

`release` silently clamps excess releases to zero via `saturating_sub`. `ship` rejects the same case with an error. This inconsistency risks hiding bugs.

`ship` subtracts `qty` from `on_hand` without checking that the stock count covers it. If `record_loss` previously left `reserved` above `on_hand`, this underflows and panics even when `qty` is within bounds.

`record_loss` also subtracts `lost` from `on_hand` without verifying the loss fits within available stock, and it ignores reserved units entirely.

`total_value` multiplies `on_hand` by `price_cents` and sums the products. This can overflow `u64` in both directions, panicking in debug or wrapping in release.

`low_stock` calls `available()` inside a filter, so it panics whenever `reserved` exceeds `on_hand`.

`moving_average` uses `assert!` to reject a zero window. This is an intentional API contract, but it may be better as a `Result` error.

The `moving_average` assert is intentional. A zero window would produce NaN from division by zero, so the guard is correct.

I am now examining `deltas`.

`deltas` panics on any non-empty input. The loop runs to `prices.len()`, but the code reads `prices[i + 1]`. When `i` reaches the final index, that access is out of bounds. Even a single-element slice triggers the panic.

`deltas` also risks signed integer overflow when subtracting `i64` prices, panicking in debug or wrapping in release.

The loop bound should be `0..prices.len().saturating_sub(1)` or `1..prices.len()` to avoid the out-of-bounds panic.

`SlotTable::lookup` uses `get_unchecked` on an untrusted scanner slot index. This is undefined behavior if the slot exceeds the table length.

`SlotTable::assign` safely rejects out-of-bounds slots, but `lookup` does not. The inconsistency is dangerous.

`append_batch` computes a raw pointer to the first element after pushing it, then extends the buffer with more elements. If the vector reallocates, that pointer becomes dangling and dereferencing it is undefined behavior.

`append_batch` also invalidates its raw pointer under Rust's aliasing rules. Deriving a pointer from a vector and then mutating that same vector with `extend_from_slice` creates a use-after-borrow violation, even if no reallocation occurs.

`append_batch` computes a raw pointer to the first element with `wrapping_add(start)`, but that pointer is immediately dereferenced after `extend_from_slice` mutates the vector. The unsafe block is completely unnecessary because the first SKU is already available as a local variable.

`encode` truncates the item name length to `u8`. A name longer than 255 bytes wraps the prefix byte and corrupts the wire format. `decode` then mis-parses the payload.

The `encode` length truncation is acceptable because the wire format comment explicitly allows it. The `Vec::with_capacity(1 + name.len() + 8)` overflow is an extreme edge case that panics or wraps without undefined behavior, so it is not a real defect.

`decode` uses `from_utf8_unchecked` on untrusted network bytes. Invalid UTF-8 triggers undefined behavior. It should use `from_utf8` and return a malformed record error.

`Service` uses three separate `Mutex` guards for the warehouse, holds map, and next ID. This creates lock ordering risks. `place_hold` acquires the warehouse lock first, then later locks the holds map and next ID mutexes. If another thread holds the holds or next ID lock while `place_hold` tries to acquire the warehouse lock, a deadlock can occur.

`confirm` acquires the `holds` lock before the `warehouse` lock, while `sweep_expired` acquires `warehouse` first. This cross-lock ordering creates a deadlock: a thread holding `holds` and waiting for `warehouse` can collide with one holding `warehouse` and waiting for `holds`.

`confirm` deletes the expired hold from the map before attempting to release its stock. If `release` fails because the SKU is missing, the hold record is already gone and the warehouse may be left inconsistent.

`confirm` deletes the hold from the map before calling `ship`. If `ship` fails because the SKU is insufficient, the hold record is already gone and the reserved units are leaked forever. The reservation becomes orphaned with no way to recover it.

`place_hold` increments the global hold ID with `*n += 1`. If the counter wraps around, the hold record is inserted into the map while the warehouse still holds the reserved stock. The reservation becomes orphaned and impossible to recover.

`place_hold` adds `ttl` to `Instant::now()` without checking for overflow. A very large duration can panic in debug or wrap in release, so the API is unsafe for untrusted input.

`receive` replaces the entire item record instead of adding to existing stock. It resets `reserved` to zero and `on_hand` to the new quantity, which silently discards prior reservations and active holds. This violates the documented behavior of adding units and leaves the warehouse in an inconsistent state.

`release` clamps excess releases to zero because it tracks total reserved stock per SKU rather than per hold. This means releasing more units than one hold actually reserved can silently steal from other active holds, so callers cannot detect the error.

`moving_average` sums daily `u32` counts into a `u64`. If the window exceeds roughly 2^32 elements, the total overflows `u64`.

The encode truncation at line 204 is silent data corruption. A name longer than 255 bytes is truncated, and decode reads the wrong slice length, so the payload is mis-parsed into an incorrect SKU and quantity.

Truncating the name length to `u8` can split a multi-byte UTF-8 character. The decoder then feeds an invalid byte sequence into `from_utf8_unchecked`, which triggers undefined behavior.

`total_value` can overflow when summing large per-unit values.

`sweep_expired` and `place_hold` both acquire the warehouse lock before the holds map, so they cannot deadlock with each other. The global hold ID starts at zero but is never used; the first valid ID is one. Mutex poisoning panics are a conventional concern and not a primary defect.

`receive` replaces the entire item record instead of adding to existing stock. It resets `reserved` to zero and `on_hand` to the new quantity, which silently discards prior reservations and active holds. This breaks the cross-function invariant that `Service` holds may still reference those reservations.

`Item` is `Clone` with public fields, so callers can set `reserved` above `on_hand` directly and corrupt the warehouse invariant.

`available()` panics when `reserved` exceeds `on_hand`. The `Item` struct exposes public fields, so callers can corrupt the invariant and trigger this panic. If `release` clamps excess releases to zero, the broken invariant can cascade into integer overflow during `reserved += qty`.

`ship` subtracts `qty` from `on_hand` before checking whether the SKU is actually in stock. If the quantity exceeds `on_hand`, the subtraction panics in debug mode or wraps in release mode.

`record_loss` subtracts the lost quantity from `on_hand` without reducing `reserved`. This leaves reserved units unaccounted for, so a later `ship` can succeed even though those reserved items are no longer in stock. If the lost amount exceeds `on_hand`, the subtraction underflows immediately.

`deltas` indexes `prices[i + 1]` without checking the bounds of the slice, so it panics when the input has fewer than two elements.

`deltas` subtracts `prices[i + 1] - prices[i]`, so the last iteration always accesses out of bounds and panics on any non-empty slice. The subtraction can also overflow `i64` when the difference exceeds `i64::MAX`.

`SlotTable::lookup` uses `get_unchecked`, so any scanner input that produces an out-of-bounds index triggers undefined behavior. Empty table lookups are also unsafe.

`SlotTable::append_batch` uses `get_unchecked` on a pointer that may be invalidated by `Vec::extend`, so any reallocation triggers undefined behavior.

`confirm` deletes the hold record before calling `ship` or `release`. If either call panics, the reservation remains orphaned and the hold is permanently lost. `release` only fails for an unknown SKU, and no code removes items from the warehouse, so a missing SKU is not a realistic failure path.

`ship` subtracts `qty` from `on_hand` after already reducing `reserved`. If the subtraction panics, the hold record is already removed from the map and the reservation is orphaned. The warehouse lock is poisoned by the panic, so the corrupted state persists.

`place_hold` acquires the warehouse lock before the holds map lock. If it panics after reserving stock but before inserting the hold record, the reservation is orphaned and the hold record is permanently lost.

The global hold ID counter is protected by a separate mutex that is never locked before the warehouse or holds locks, so it cannot deadlock. All internal state is guarded by Mutexes and the Service type is Sync.

`place_hold` acquires the warehouse lock before the holds map lock. Because `Mutex` is not reentrant, a thread that already holds the warehouse lock cannot acquire the holds lock while it still holds the warehouse lock. This creates a deadlock if any internal function tries to acquire the holds map lock while holding the warehouse lock.

`sweep_expired` calls `holds.retain` while holding the warehouse lock. The closure may invoke `release`, which acquires the holds map lock, so the two locks are acquired in a different order than in `confirm`. This creates a deadlock risk.

`parse_command` rejects negative numbers and trailing tokens, but it does not reject empty input or a missing quantity.

`moving_average` panics when the window is zero because it uses an `assert!` instead of returning a `Result`. The loop bounds are correct.

`record_loss` does not check that the lost quantity is within `on_hand`, so it can panic or underflow when the loss exceeds available stock. It also never checks whether the loss would exceed the reserved count, which lets the `reserved <= on_hand` invariant break even when the loss is valid.

`place_hold` can overflow `Instant` when adding the hold duration to the current time, causing the hold to expire immediately.

The global hold ID counter can overflow, but this is practically unreachable and will be omitted from the ISSUES list.

`release` clamps excess releases to zero instead of erroring, so it can silently clear other reservations and hide a logic bug. The documentation does not specify this behavior.

`confirm` deletes the hold record before `ship` or `release` succeeds. If either call panics, the reservation is orphaned and the hold is permanently lost.

`place_hold` does not reject a zero quantity, so it creates a hold record that immediately expires. `confirm` then treats that expired hold as an immediate success and ships the items.

`encode` silently truncates item names longer than 255 bytes by casting the length to `u8`. `decode` uses unsafe UTF-8 conversion at line 218.

`low_stock` calls `i.available()` without handling the panic that `available()` can raise when `reserved` exceeds `on_hand`.

`moving_average` can overflow its `u64` sum when the window is large enough to require more than roughly 4.3 billion elements. This is a real integer overflow defect.

`receive` replaces the entire item instead of adding to its existing `on_hand`, and it zeroes `reserved`. `total_value` can overflow its `u64` sum when multiplied quantities are large.

`moving_average` uses an explicit `assert!` on a zero window, so it panics deliberately rather than returning an error. This will be described as an intentional contract check in the prose but omitted from the ISSUES list to avoid style nits.

Deadlocks are unrecoverable because the service never attempts lock poisoning recovery. `confirm` also releases expired holds while still holding the `holds` map lock, so a failed release leaves the reservation orphaned.

`confirm` returns `UnknownSku` instead of `Expired` when a hold is already expired, so callers cannot distinguish an expired hold from a missing SKU.

The `deltas` loop does not actually panic on the last index. Because `i` stops at `len - 1`, `i + 1` never exceeds `usize::MAX`, so the out-of-bounds concern is invalid. The display format string also correctly uses a literal dot for the price separator, and truncation of long names is not a bug.

Under Stacked Borrows, `Vec::extend_from_slice` retags the entire allocation and invalidates any raw pointers created from a shared borrow. The pointer from `append_batch` becomes undefined behavior even when no reallocation occurs, because the unique borrow of the vector invalidates the earlier shared borrow.

The Rust documentation and Nomicon suggest that raw pointers become invalid only when a vector reallocated, not merely because a unique borrow was taken. This casts doubt on whether `append_batch`'s pointer is actually undefined behavior under Stacked Borrows.

Miri and the Rustonomicon confirm that `Vec::extend_from_slice` retags the entire allocation and invalidates any raw pointers derived from a shared borrow. The pointer from `append_batch` is therefore undefined behavior, even when no reallocation occurs.

The `append_batch` pointer is undefined behavior whenever the vector reallocates, which happens in the common case because `extend_from_slice` grows the buffer whenever capacity is tight. This makes it a practical bug even if it does not panic on every call.

The `receive` log message is also misleading: it prints `receive x{qty}` even when the SKU already exists and the call replaces the item rather than adding to its quantity.

Line 80 is the exact spot where the replacement item is built with `on_hand` set to `qty` and `reserved` zeroed. The `deltas` loop will be listed as two separate issues: one for the out-of-bounds read and one for the i64 subtraction overflow.

The `append_batch` invalid pointer is dereferenced at line 196, so that is the precise defect line. The `deltas` out-of-bounds read and i64 subtraction overflow are kept as two separate issues. The deadlock is cited at line 259 because it follows the inverted lock order of holds before warehouse; the related `place_hold` and `sweep_expired` calls are noted in the description. The premature hold removal is listed at line 260.

The `sweep_expired` error discard at line 278 is omitted because the SKU always exists and `release` returns `Ok` in practice. The `reserved += qty` addition at line 96 is also skipped since it only overflows if the invariant is already broken.

The `ship` subtraction at line 112 is a consequence of `record_loss` at line 120, not an independent defect. Because `reserve` only allows quantities up to the available stock, the invariant that `reserved <= on_hand` is maintained unless `record_loss` or `receive` breaks it.

`ship` at line 112 is kept as a separate issue because it panics once the invariant breaks, unlike `record_loss` which only wraps. `available` at line 47 is also kept because it is the primitive that panics; in debug builds this exposes broken invariants, while release builds wrap to a huge value and let `reserve` overflow `reserved` further.

The review will be organized by severity, with undefined behavior first, then panics and overflow, then logic defects, then concurrency issues. The ISSUES list will be sorted by line number as requested. The `append_batch` invalid pointer is confirmed safe because the slice is built before reallocation; the real risk is stacked borrows when `extend_from_slice` reallocates.

`append_batch` is practically unsafe because `push` often exhausts capacity, forcing reallocation that triggers stacked borrows. `decode` uses `from_utf8_unchecked`, which the Rust docs explicitly label as undefined behavior for invalid bytes.

The `deltas` loop is an off-by-one error: the author intended `n-1` outputs because capacity is `saturating_sub(1)`, but the loop runs over the full slice length.

The lock-order analysis is being tightened. Only `confirm` and `sweep_expired` can deadlock because they acquire the holds mutex before the warehouse mutex, while `snapshot` and `place_hold` acquire warehouse first. `place_hold` also locks `next_id` inside its critical section, which widens the critical section but does not introduce a new deadlock.

`saturating_sub` in `release` makes over-release indistinguishable from success, so callers may believe they freed more stock than they actually did. `record_loss` also fails to reduce `reserved`, leaving orphaned reservations that can later be shipped and corrupt inventory accounting.

The review is now complete. Public fields are treated as a real safety hole rather than a style nit, because direct mutation could break the `available()` invariant.

`total_value` can overflow `u64` during per-item multiplication or summation. The `deltas` loop reads `prices[i + 1]` without bounds checking, so it panics on every non-empty input. Day-over-day subtraction in that same loop can overflow `i64`, panicking in debug builds and wrapping silently in release. `lookup` uses `get_unchecked` on an untrusted scanner index, which triggers undefined behavior for out-of-range slots. `append_batch` dereferences a pointer into its buffer after `extend_from_slice`, so reallocation leaves the pointer dangling.

The review is finalized at 15 issues. `encode` truncates SKU names longer than 255 bytes by casting `name.len()` to `u8`. `Instant::now() + ttl` panics when the expiry overflows, after `reserve` has already committed the hold. `confirm` removes the hold before calling `release` or `ship`, so a failure in either leaves reserved units orphaned.
